common_name: October Glory Red Maple (Late-Season Brilliant Red Fall Color Maple)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; October Glory holds its leaves and colors later into fall than most red maples, giving a late burst of brilliant red color after other trees have already dropped their leaves.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. October Glory is one of the most widely planted red maple cultivars for its dependable, long-lasting, brilliant red fall color that develops later in the season than most maples, extending the fall color display after earlier-turning trees have already gone bare. It grows at a moderate-to-fast rate into a dense, rounded shade tree and tolerates a wider range of soil conditions, including occasional wet sites, than many other shade trees, making it a versatile choice for yards, streets, and parks. Like other red maples it has relatively shallow, fibrous roots that can compete with grass and nearby plantings, so avoid heavy underplanting close to the trunk and keep it well watered during establishment and drought.

common_name: Autumn Blaze Maple (Fast-Growing Hybrid Freeman Maple)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumn Blaze is a hybrid of silver and red maple combining the fast growth of silver maple with the stronger wood and fall color of red maple.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Autumn Blaze is a hybrid cross between silver maple and red maple, bred to combine the rapid growth rate of silver maple with the sturdier branch structure and reliable orange-red fall color of red maple, avoiding the weak, storm-prone wood that has made straight silver maple less popular as a landscape tree. It grows into a dense, oval-to-rounded shade tree relatively quickly compared to most large shade trees, making it a popular choice where gardeners want a mature-looking canopy sooner rather than later. It is adaptable to a range of soils and tolerates urban conditions reasonably well, though like its silver maple parent it can have somewhat brittle wood in ice or heavy wind, and should be kept away from underground utilities and pavement given its vigorous surface roots.

common_name: Drake Chinese Elm (Semi-Evergreen Gulf South Shade Tree)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Drake Chinese elm is fast-growing, tolerates heat, drought, and urban conditions well, and is resistant to Dutch elm disease, unlike American elm.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Drake is a graceful, fast-growing selection of Chinese elm valued for its attractive mottled, exfoliating bark, fine-textured foliage, and semi-evergreen habit that holds leaves later into fall and winter than most deciduous shade trees across much of the Gulf South. Unlike American elm, it shows strong resistance to Dutch elm disease and also tolerates heat, drought, and compacted urban soils well, making it a popular street and shade tree throughout Texas and the Deep South. Its arching, weeping branch habit gives mature specimens an elegant silhouette, and it needs only routine structural pruning when young to develop strong branch angles for long-term storm resistance.

common_name: Allee Lacebark Elm (Texas A&M Drought-Tolerant Shade Tree)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Allee was selected by Texas A&M for its uniform vase-shaped form, striking exfoliating bark, and excellent heat and drought tolerance for southern shade tree use.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Allee is a lacebark elm cultivar selected and introduced by Texas A&M University for its uniform, vase-shaped growth habit, resembling the classic silhouette of American elm without the vulnerability to Dutch elm disease that devastated that species. Its most striking feature is the beautifully mottled, exfoliating bark in patches of gray, green, orange, and brown that develops as the tree matures, giving significant year-round ornamental interest even in winter. It is highly tolerant of heat, drought, and the alkaline, compacted soils common in urban and suburban Southern landscapes, requiring only routine structural pruning while young to establish strong branch angles for a long-lived, storm-resistant shade tree.

common_name: Shawnee Brave Bald Cypress (Narrow Columnar Bald Cypress)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shawnee Brave is a narrow, columnar selection of bald cypress that fits street and boulevard plantings where the broader native species would need more room.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, though established trees also tolerate average well-drained garden soil once roots are developed. Shawnee Brave is a narrow, densely pyramidal selection of the native Southern bald cypress, holding a much more upright, columnar shape than the broadly spreading wild species, which makes it far better suited to street plantings, narrow side yards, and formal allees where space is limited. Like the species, it tolerates both flooded and ordinary garden soil with equal ease, developing the picturesque flared trunk base and soft, ferny, deciduous foliage that turns rusty orange-brown in fall before dropping. It is highly wind- and storm-resistant once established and essentially free of serious pests or diseases, making it an excellent long-lived specimen or street tree throughout the Gulf South.
